chunks.text: 2 Methods In this section we introduce the MPI reconstruction problem based on a system matrix (Section 2.1 ). We recall the main data preprocessing steps typically employed (Section 2.2 ) and, finally, introduce the MPISuperRes-PnP algorithm in Section 2.3 . 2.1 System-Matrix-Based Reconstruction in MPI In MPI the target concentration of nanoparticles ρ GT \rho_{\mathrm{GT}} is to be reconstructed from the measured signal f f . In the system-matrix-based approach, the problem is considered in a discrete (spatial) scenario. Consequently, in a two-dimensional setup, the field-of-view (FoV) Ω \Omega is discretized by considering an N x × N y N_{x}\times N_{y} grid. We denote with N = N x ⋅ N y N=N_{x}\cdot N_{y} the total number of grid cells. With this discretization, the target concentration ρ GT \rho_{\mathrm{GT}} is approximated by a vector x ∈ ℝ N x\in\mathbb{R}^{N} such that ρ GT ≈ x ~ ∈ ℝ N x × N y \rho_{\mathrm{GT}}\approx\tilde{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{x}\times N_{y}} where ⋅ ~ \tilde{\cdot} is the reshaping operator; additionally, the relation with the signal f f is modeled via the relation f = A ​ x + η f=Ax+\eta (1) where the symbol A ∈ ℝ M × N A\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N} denotes the system matrix and η \eta represents the inherent noise in the measurement [ 21 ] . In the measurement-based approach, the system matrix A A is acquired via a calibration procedure performed by iteratively scanning and repositioning a known concentration of nanoparticles (the δ \delta -concentration) across each cell of the N x × N y N_{x}\times N_{y} grid. We point out that A A is the of size M × N M\times N , where N = N x × N y N=N_{x}\times N_{y} as defined above, and M M is the number of rows, which depends on the number of channels employed and on the preprocessing applied to the data before solving the linear system in ( 1 ) (cf. section 2.2 ).

As an example, in the 2D OpenMPI [ 49 ] the calibration is performed on a 19 × 19 19\times 19 grid, yielding N = 19 2 = 361 N=19^{2}=361 , and each scan is acquired at 1632 1632 time points along two channels (with coils positioned along the x x - and y y -axis) and Fourier transformed, giving 817 817 complex-valued frequencies per channel; upon stacking of the real and imaginary parts per channel to obtain a real-valued matrix, the total amount of rows is M = 2 ⋅ 2 ⋅ 817 = 3268 M=2\cdot 2\cdot 817=3268 . Finally, given a scan f f and a calibration matrix A A , the objective is to retrieve x x solving ( 1 ). Because both f f and A A are affected by real noise, the inversion of ( 1 ) requires regularization techniques [ 50 , 51 ] . 2.2 Data Preprocessing Usual preprocessing steps performed on MPI data affect the number of rows M M of the linear system in ( 1 ). The reason is that these preprocessing steps are usually aimed at either improving the conditioning of the system in ( 1 ) or at discarding unreliable frequencies, that are deemed as such according to chosen criteria. We recall the main preprocessing steps as, for instance, outlined in [ 52 ] . i) Background Correction : according to the models, the measured data can be decomposed as f = f cl . + b f + η f f=f_{\mathrm{cl.}}+b_{f}+\eta_{f} and coherently the system matrix as A = A cl . + b A + η A A=A_{\mathrm{cl.}}+b_{A}+\eta_{A} , where f cl . f_{\mathrm{cl.}} , S cl . S_{\mathrm{cl.}} are the clean signals, b f b_{f} , b A b_{A} are the background signals and η f \eta_{f} , η A \eta_{A} are the arrays representing the noise. To exclude the background signals, which bear no information about the underlying particle concentrations, empty scans without any particles in the scanner are performed at the time of calibration as well as before or after the scan of the target specimen. These background scans can be subtracted form A A and f f to correct for the background terms.

ii) Bandpass Filtering : some scanners (like the Bruker scanner) utilize an analog filter to suppress excitation crosstalk – at the price of decreasing the Signal-to-Noise ratio (SNR) – of frequencies below 80 ​ kHz 80\ $\mathrm{kHz}$ [ 29 ] . For this reason, a high-pass filter at 80 ​ kHz 80\ $\mathrm{kHz}$ is usually necessary. iii) SNR-Thresholding : provided an estimation of the SNR of each frequency is available, SNR-based thresholding is usually performed [ 52 ] by discarding those frequencies whose SNR is below a certain threshold Θ \Theta , e.g., below Θ = 1 ​ dB \Theta=1\ $\mathrm{dB}$ . iv) Whitening : in [ 53 ] the authors have proposed to apply a whitening transformation, i.e., considering the whitened system W ​ A ​ x = W ​ f WAx=Wf where the matrix W ∈ ℝ M × M W\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times M} is the diagonal covariance matrix obtained from background scans. More specifically, the diagonal entries of W W are the terms 1 / σ b 1/\sigma_{b} and σ b 2 \sigma_{b}^{2} is the variance of the background scan. v) Low Rank Approximation : following [ 52 ] , a target rank K ≤ min ⁡ { M , n } K\leq\min\{M,n\} can be selected and a randomized singular value decomposition (rSVD) [ 54 ] is performed. The output of the rSVD is a triple of matrix ( U K , Σ K , V K ) (U_{K},\Sigma_{K},V_{K}) such that A ≈ U K ​ Σ K ​ V K ∗ A\approx U_{K}\Sigma_{K}V_{K}^{*} . By employing U K U_{K} , the system with K K rows, U K ∗ ​ A ​ x = U K ∗ ​ f U^{*}_{K}Ax=U_{K}^{*}f , is then considered. 2.3 MPISuperRes-PnP: an Algorithm for Super-Resolved Regularized Inversion with Zero-Shot Learned-Denoiser In this section we introduce MPISuperRes-PnP, the proposed algorithm to incorporate super-resolution within the ZeroShot-PnP framework in [ 44 ] .

In view of these similarities, we employ the benchmark deep denoiser prior [ 42 ] as denoiser in ( 10 ), because the deep denoiser prior can take noise level maps as additional input. We adapt also the automatic update strategy proposed in [ 44 ] for μ k \mu_{k} . We now provide more details to elucidate these statements. The backbone architecture of the deep denoiser prior [ 42 ] is the DRUNet, a deep CNN architecture which combines a U-Net [ 55 ] with the ResNet [ 56 ] . The deep denoiser prior has been trained on a combination of various dataset such as the Waterloo Exploration Database [ 57 ] , BSD [ 58 ] , Flick2K [ 59 ] and DIV2K [ 60 ] . The denoiser is publicly available at https://github.com/cszn/DPIR and was trained as follows: the authors of [ 42 ] randomly cropped out 16 patches of size 128 × 128 128\times 128 , selected a random noise level σ \sigma chosen from [ 0 , 50 ] [0,50] and added additive Gaussian noise with level σ \sigma .

Additionally, a map filled uniformly with the value σ \sigma and of the same size as the image has been provided as noise level map. The range [ 0 , 50 ] [0,50] has been chosen to account for large variations of the noise level. For completeness we also mention that the DRUNet consists of 32,638,656 trainable parameters. We remark that the deep denoiser prior is used in MPISuperRes-PnP in a zero-shot fashion, that means it is used without further training nor fine-tuning on MPI-specific nor MPI-related data. As mentioned above, the parameters in ( 9 ) and ( 10 ) are coupled and consequently, it is reasonable to take this into account when choosing the denoiser. We have seen that the deep denoiser prior has been designed in such a way that noise level maps can be set as inputs in the denoising, de facto allowing to perform denoising with a prescribed parameter in ( 10 ). In particular, in section 3.1 we describe the datasets employed: the MPI-MNIST dataset [ 46 , 47 ] , our own MPI-CHAR dataset, the OpenMPI dataset [ 49 ] , and the “Equilibrium Model with Anisotropy” dataset [ 48 ] . In section 3.2 we describe the image quality measures employed to quantitatively evaluate the quality of the reconstructions. The reconstructions performed on the four datasets are described in the respective sections 3.3 , 3.4 , 3.5 , and 3.6 . The MPISuperRes-PnP algorithm and the proprocessing of the data have been implemented in Python 3.9, using Numpy and PyTorch. The reconstructions were performed on a workstation with 13th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i9-13900KS, 128 GB of RAM, an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU and Windows 11 Pro. 3.1 Datasets In this work we test the MPISuperRes-PnP algorithm on a variety of simulated and real dataset, which we here describe: 1. The MPI-MNIST [ 46 , 47 ] is a recently published dataset of simulated MPI measurements obtained using state-of-the-art model-based system matrices. In addition, the dataset employs real noise measurements obtained from a real MPI scanner. In particular, the dataset contains simulated system matrices A N x × N y A_{N_{x}\times N_{y}} for three different resolutions, namely, for ( N x , N y ) (N_{x},N_{y}) either ( 15 , 17 ) (15,17) , ( 45 , 51 ) (45,51) or ( 75 , 85 ) (75,85) . The ground truths of this dataset have been generated in the following manner: the 28 × 28 28\times 28 images of the hand written digits in the MNIST dataset are first downsampled to a 11 × 11 11\times 11 pixel grid with the nearest neighbor interpolation scheme and padded with zeros to get to the size of 15 × 17 15\times 17 pixels. The resulting 15 × 17 15\times 17 -sized images are upscaled to the 75 × 85 75\times 85 grid using nearest neighbor interpolation.

Finally, the scan signal y y is obtained for each ground truth x x as y = A 75 × 85 ​ x + η y=A_{75\times 85}x+\eta (12) where η \eta is an instance of real noise collected with a real scanner. 2. We observe that in the MPI-MNIST dataset the ground truths are natively on a 15 × 17 15\times 17 grid and upscaled to the 75 × 85 75\times 85 grid using nearest neighbors interpolation. As a consequence, the features of the ground truth live on the 15 × 17 15\times 17 and no more fine-grained features are to be gained from reconstructing the phantom on a 75 × 85 75\times 85 grid. It follows that the MPI-MNIST data set is limited for testing super-resolution algorithms since it does not carry fine level details. For this reason, we have created the MPI-CHAR dataset. The MPI-CHAR dataset is a simulated dataset created using the data-generation methodology of the MPI-MNIST dataset, but using a set of ground truths with higher native resolution. More specifically, characters from an openly available font 1 1 1 Liberation Sans Font Regular is licensed under GNU general public license (GPL) and available at https://www.1001fonts.com/liberation-sans-font.html . have been used to create ground truths on a 75 × 85 75\times 85 grid; these ground truths have been used to generate signals following the methodology of the MPI-MNIST dataset, i.e., applying the forward operator A 75 × 85 A_{75\times 85} and adding real noise as in ( 12 ). The matrix A 75 × 85 A_{75\times 85} and the noise instances are the one published in the MPI-MNIST dataset. 3. The OpenMPI dataset [ 49 ] is a benchmark dataset, which contains real 1D, 2D and 3D scan data of 3 phantoms obtained with a Bruker scanner. Here, we use the 2D scan data and 2D system matrices. The dataset contains system matrices in two different resolutions: a 19 × 19 19\times 19 lower resolution and a 37 × 37 37\times 37 higher resolution system matrix.

The presence of a higher resolution system matrix allows us to compare higher resolution reconstructions of real phantoms with the ones obtained with the MPISuperRes-PnP method. 4. The Equilibrium Model with Anisotropy dataset (EMWA dataset) of [ 48 ] contains real 2D scan data of 6 phantoms obtained with a Bruker scanner. In this dataset, the system matrix provided has been calibrated on a 15 × 17 15\times 17 grid. The dataset does not offer a higher resolution system matrix. Nevertheless, we provide reconstructions on this dataset to further test the MPISuperRes-PnP algorithm on real MPI data. The Open-MPI and the EMWA datasets contain real MPI scans and are used in this paper to provide a qualitative evaluation of the method on real data. The MPI-MNIST and the MPI-CHAR datasets are simulated (with real noise) and contain ground truths. These are used to compute quality metrics and provide a quantitative evaluation of the method. In section 3.1 we argue that the MPI-MNIST dataset is not properly suitable to test super-resolution because of the way the dataset is produced. We recall briefly that the ground truths in the MPI-MNIST dataset live natively on a 15 × 17 15\times 17 grid and are upscaled by nearest neighbors when producing the data scans.

The MPI-MNIST [ 46 , 47 ] is a recently published dataset of simulated MPI measurements obtained using state-of-the-art model-based system matrices. In addition, the dataset employs real noise measurements obtained from a real MPI scanner. In particular, the dataset contains simulated system matrices A N x × N y A_{N_{x}\times N_{y}} for three different resolutions, namely, for ( N x , N y ) (N_{x},N_{y}) either ( 15 , 17 ) (15,17) , ( 45 , 51 ) (45,51) or ( 75 , 85 ) (75,85) . The ground truths of this dataset have been generated in the following manner: the 28 × 28 28\times 28 images of the hand written digits in the MNIST dataset are first downsampled to a 11 × 11 11\times 11 pixel grid with the nearest neighbor interpolation scheme and padded with zeros to get to the size of 15 × 17 15\times 17 pixels. The resulting 15 × 17 15\times 17 -sized images are upscaled to the 75 × 85 75\times 85 grid using nearest neighbor interpolation. Finally, the scan signal y y is obtained for each ground truth x x as y = A 75 × 85 ​ x + η y=A_{75\times 85}x+\eta (12) where η \eta is an instance of real noise collected with a real scanner. 2. We observe that in the MPI-MNIST dataset the ground truths are natively on a 15 × 17 15\times 17 grid and upscaled to the 75 × 85 75\times 85 grid using nearest neighbors interpolation. As a consequence, the features of the ground truth live on the 15 × 17 15\times 17 and no more fine-grained features are to be gained from reconstructing the phantom on a 75 × 85 75\times 85 grid. It follows that the MPI-MNIST data set is limited for testing super-resolution algorithms since it does not carry fine level details. For this reason, we have created the MPI-CHAR dataset.
